opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing is that these large models, as they currently stand, are fundamentally mimicking the data they've been trained on. They're extraordinarily good at that. They can blend ideas, interpolate between things they've seen, and that can look quite creative at times. But if you want something genuinely new, something that isn't just a recombination of patterns in the training distribution, you need a way to explore the space of possibilities and find things that work.

The classic example, which I think about a lot, is AlphaGo and move 37. That move wasn't in the human data. If you had just trained a model to predict what strong human players do, it would have assigned that move a very low probability, maybe one in ten thousand. AlphaGo found it because it combined a learned model of the game with search. It could look ahead, evaluate positions, and discover that this strange-looking move was actually very strong. That's real creativity in a meaningful sense: finding something valuable that nobody had found before.

So I think a similar thing has to happen with these more general systems. You have a very rich model of the world, which the large language models are giving us, and then on top of that you need the ability to search over possibilities, try out ideas, check them against some notion of what's good or correct, and iterate. Humans do this too. When a mathematician is working on a hard problem, they're not just blurting out the most likely next line. They're exploring, trying approaches, backtracking, seeing what works.

The hard part, of course, is that Go has a very clean objective. You know who won. In open-ended domains, defining what a good outcome is, and searching efficiently in an enormous space, is much harder. But I think that combination, powerful learned models plus search and some way of evaluating results, is what will take us from systems that reflect human knowledge back at us to systems that can actually extend it.

r001.rationale: It says search explores possibilities and finds what works, using AlphaGo’s overlooked but valuable move 37 as an example.

r002.rationale: It contrasts blending or recombining learned patterns with finding something genuinely new beyond the training distribution.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that a model trained purely on existing data is, in a sense, bounded by that data. It's learning the distribution of what humans have already written, already discovered, already thought. And it can interpolate within that very well, it can recombine things in interesting ways. But if you want to go genuinely beyond, to find something that isn't in the training distribution at all, you need some mechanism for exploring and then selecting. That's what search gives you.

The clearest example of this is AlphaGo and then AlphaZero. AlphaGo was initially trained on human games. It got to roughly expert level that way. But the famous move 37 in the Lee Sedol match, that wasn't something it imitated from a human. That came from the combination of the learned model and the search process, the Monte Carlo tree search exploring possibilities and finding something that human players had basically dismissed. And then with AlphaZero, you remove the human data entirely, and it goes well past the best humans, and it finds novel openings and strategies that the Go community then studied. So that's a very concrete case where search plus learning produces things that no amount of imitation alone would produce.

I think the deeper point is that creativity, if you look at how it actually works in humans, isn't magic either. A scientist or a mathematician or a composer generates candidate ideas, evaluates them, discards most of them, refines the promising ones. That's search. It might be quite a sophisticated, heuristic, intuition-guided search, but structurally that's what's going on. The learned model provides the intuition, the sense of which directions are worth exploring. The search provides the actual exploration into new territory. If you only have the intuition, you're stuck with what you already know. If you only have blind search, you're hopelessly inefficient in any interesting space. You need both.

So when people ask me whether large language models can be creative, my answer is that the base model on its own is doing something closer to sophisticated recall and recombination. To get the kind of creativity where you discover genuinely new mathematics or new science, you need to wrap that model in a process that proposes, tests against some ground truth or some evaluator, and iterates. Otherwise you're always going to be, at best, as good as the best of what's in the data. And that's a ceiling I don't think we want.

r001.rationale: The response says search explores possibilities and selects promising ones, using AlphaGo’s move 37 as an example of a valuable possibility human players had dismissed.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes recombining learned material from discovering something outside the training distribution, and says search enables that further exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between recognizing a good solution and being able to produce one. You might be able to look at a mathematical proof and understand why it works, but that doesn’t mean you can immediately come up with that proof. You have to try things, follow some paths that don’t work, and use what you learn to guide the next attempt.

Training gives you a very powerful basis for that process. You learn patterns, useful abstractions, and intuitions about which directions are promising. But when you encounter a genuinely difficult new problem, you want to be able to spend more computation on it—to explore possibilities and test them—rather than being limited to whatever answer comes out immediately.

Now, I wouldn’t say that a system without explicit search can never create anything new. It can combine things it has learned in novel ways, and some search might happen implicitly in its computation. But I suspect that for the kinds of creativity we care about in science and mathematics, you need that iterative process. The learned model helps you search intelligently, and search lets you get further than your initial intuition.

r001.rationale: The response says search explores and tests possibilities to get beyond the immediate answer and initial intuition, conveying that it can find promising options that would otherwise be missed.

r002.rationale: It explicitly allows novel combinations of learned material without explicit search, then distinguishes that from the iterative search it says is needed for creativity in science and mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between recognizing a good answer and being able to produce one immediately. You can look at a mathematical proof and see that it works, but that doesn’t mean you could have written it down in one shot. You may need to try different approaches, follow their consequences, discover that some don’t work, and go back.

Training can give a system very powerful intuitions about which directions are promising. But when you’re facing a genuinely new problem, those intuitions may not take you all the way to a solution. Search lets you spend additional computation exploring possibilities and evaluating them, rather than relying entirely on what you can produce in a single pass.

I wouldn’t say that a system without explicit search can’t create anything new. It clearly can combine things in novel ways. But for creativity that involves finding something both surprising and deeply constrained—a new algorithm, for example—I think that ability to explore and check possibilities becomes very important.

r001.rationale: The response says search lets a system explore and evaluate possibilities beyond a single-pass answer, including paths its intuitions may not reach.

r002.rationale: It contrasts novel combinations with creativity on a genuinely new problem, but does not clearly identify those combinations as learned material or state that the latter goes beyond that material.
